summary: Human skin of one measured tone between types III and IV: a complete 8K set with its own shine maps, the lips worn on the skin.
_comment: SUBJECT Tone34 (Phase24 One Validated Skin, RD-P24-1 ... 8): one person's complete skin set beside the six Fitzpatrick tones, judged against a scanned reference skin on the same body (the reference is research only and never ships, RD-SKM-2, RD-P23-10). The Variant names the measured tone, between III and IV (RD-P24-8), never a person. All five maps are the article's own, 4096 square on hm08's 2048 layout since 2026-11-02 (the lead: "4k or even 2k is fine right now"; 8192 before, RD-OVS-2, RD-P24-2). Colour: gen_skin_maps.py --subject Tone34 (the pigment maker on IV's fitted response at the subject's own melanin, its placed face colour and lips solved against the reference's same regions; the face core held at the reference's mean there). Shine: gen_skin_shine.py --subject Tone34 (the shared design at 8K, one height sample a texel; the cavity map's level per face region and on the lips fitted to the reference's specular; the lips' roughness 0.30). THE LIPS WEAR THIS ARTICLE (RD-P24-3): there is no Lips_Tone34; the lip colour is the map's and the lip gloss the roughness map's, with no coat (RD-P22-17). Every other value is Skin_FitzpatrickIII's (Physically Based Skin III: IOR, roughness), except the subsurface: radius 0.00241 (III's halved) and anisotropy 0, since 2026-11-02 (the lead in Studio: "the SSS is WWWWAAAAAYYYYY too much... basically see through"; Unreal's Substrate reads the anisotropy as opacity 1 - |g|, so III's 0.8 drew a thin, see-through surface; Storm ignores it, Blender honours it); fuzz_color is the subject's tone.
name: Skin_Tone34_Clean_Base_s001_v01

sources.note: the subject's colour map at 8192 (Phase24): CC0 parts only (MPFB2's region masks, hm08, seeded 3D melanin and blood fields through OMF's tabulated two-chromophore model; RD-SKM-2), no picture of a person; a handful of region averages measured on a research reference set its numbers (gen_synth_skin.SUBJECTS), as a tone is; base_color_const is the face core's measured mean x the map's peak factor
the subject's own roughness, normal, cavity and scatter maps at 8192 (Phase24)
Skin III's non-colour values (IOR, roughness, the scatter radius and its scale); the colour is the subject's measured tone, not this entry's

sources.why: subsurface_weight 1.0 and subsurface_color = the albedo: skin scatters throughout, and OpenPBR's default subsurface colour (light grey) would desaturate the tone. Phase21 (RD-P21-1, RD-P21-4): the scatter colour now FOLLOWS the base (subsurface_color connected to base_color_out), so it takes the map and the tint; before, it was pinned to the albedo and the tint was inert on skin in every tool (F-P21-3).

Phase22 (RD-P22-17, after click 2: "the shine is still just really over the top"): NO COAT. Phase07 7.3 gave the skin MPFB2's 'enhanced skin' clearcoat (0.1 at roughness 0.3, IOR 1.5) for its oil; on the relief it laid one sharp, wet glint over the whole body, and it double-counted the oil the roughness map's T-zone already carries. The skin's oil and its overall roughness (the map's average, 0.62) are in roughness_map. subsurface_scatter_anisotropy 0.8: tissue scatters strongly forward (a Henyey-Greenstein g of ~0.8 for skin). Fuzz 0.1 in the skin's own albedo, roughness 0.5: fine vellus hair seen at grazing angles, taking roughly the skin's hue (a light grey would put a grey rim on the darker tones); MPFB2 carries no fuzz, so the weight is kept low. Storm ignores the anisotropy (Learnings Storm S8), which adds ~1.2 to the rig's ΔE; Blender is the one honouring it.
